paragraphs: Learning systems that serve many users often improve their decisions by observing feedback from individual people. This paper studies how online learning can proceed when that individual feedback is unavailable. It introduces anonymous bandits, a framework in which the learner must make decisions and improve over time using observations that combine rewards from multiple users.

The central requirement is k-anonymity: every observation aggregates rewards from at least k users. This changes what information the learning algorithm can access. It must draw useful conclusions from group feedback rather than directly inspect a particular user's decision. Within this framework, the authors show that a clustering of users can be learned online while respecting that observation constraint.

The paper provides the first algorithms with sublinear regret for this setting, along with lower bounds. Sublinear regret means that accumulated learning-related loss grows more slowly than the interaction horizon, so its average contribution decreases. The lower bounds complement those algorithms by establishing limits on achievable performance under anonymous observations.
neurips-2022-anonymous-bandits-for-multi.tldr: Anonymous bandits enable online learning and user clustering from aggregated rewards, with sublinear regret under a k-anonymity constraint.

paragraphs: A decision tree can be easy to follow yet still require many attributes to explain a prediction. This paper introduces explanation size as an additional measure of interpretability: how sparse the set of attributes needed to explain a classification is. It complements familiar structural measures such as tree size and the average or maximum depth of leaves.

The authors study the best guarantees achievable when optimizing explanation size together with depth. Their algorithm achieves an O(ln n) approximation for both average and worst-case explanation size, as well as average and worst-case depth. The paper characterizes these guarantees as tight, with approximation optimality conditional on P not equaling NP. This gives a theoretical account of how well these interpretability objectives can be optimized.

Experiments on 20 real datasets report accuracy competitive with CART while yielding substantially simpler explanations. The findings suggest that explicitly optimizing the attributes needed for explanation can improve interpretability without sacrificing competitive predictive performance in those evaluations.
neurips-2022-decision-trees-with-short-e.tldr: The paper introduces attribute-based explanation size and an approximation algorithm that produces simpler decision-tree explanations with competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Linear sketches summarize fast-moving data streams so that useful questions can be answered without retaining the full stream. Applications include estimating item frequencies, identifying approximately the most frequent items, and summarizing distributions. When the stream contains sensitive information, those summaries also need privacy guarantees while remaining accurate enough to serve their purpose.

This paper shows that adding a small amount of noise when a linear sketch is initialized can provide differential privacy while retaining the sketch's distinctive properties. The contribution connects privacy protection with the existing sketching machinery, rather than treating privacy and efficient stream processing as separate goals. The authors also provide theoretical bounds supporting useful results from the private summaries.

As an application, the paper makes a state-of-the-art quantile sketch private in the turnstile model while maintaining high performance. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets find that the private sketches resemble noise-free sketches both quantitatively and qualitatively. These results support the practical usefulness of the proposed initialization-based approach.
neurips-2022-differentially-private-line.tldr: Adding a small amount of noise at initialization makes linear sketches differentially private while preserving useful stream-summary performance.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning depends on reward feedback to improve the decisions of interacting agents. Reliable feedback can be expensive or unavailable, leaving substantial uncertainty in the training signal. This paper addresses that problem with DRE-MARL, a framework that actively estimates reward distributions to support more effective and stable policy learning.

The method has two main components. Multi-action-branch reward estimation models reward distributions across all action branches, keeping track of possible outcomes associated with different choices. Policy-weighted aggregation then combines reward information into signals used to update the learner. The motivation is that considering the range of possible action consequences could help policy learning when observed rewards are uncertain.

Experiments in benchmark multi-agent scenarios report better effectiveness and robustness than the state-of-the-art baselines used in the study. These findings support the combination of distributional estimation and aggregation as a way to manage uncertain rewards. The reported gains concern those evaluated scenarios, while the broader contribution is a training framework built around richer reward estimates.
neurips-2022-distributional-reward-estim.tldr: DRE-MARL estimates reward distributions across action branches and aggregates them to improve multi-agent learning under reward uncertainty.

paragraphs: An agent pursuing a long-term goal may receive little feedback until it succeeds, making useful behavior difficult to discover. EAGER addresses this sparse-reward problem in reinforcement learning guided by language. It uses the language goal to automatically construct auxiliary objectives that provide additional feedback during exploration.

A question-generation system creates questions about parts of the overall goal. A question-answering system then tries to recover the relevant information using the agent's own trajectory. When it succeeds, the agent receives an intrinsic reward proportional to confidence in the answer. This encourages behavior whose trajectory clearly reveals aspects of the requested goal, connecting the additional rewards to the instruction the agent is supposed to follow.

Experiments across several BabyAI environments show improved sample efficiency through more effective exploration. The auxiliary objectives do not require an engineer to design them individually. The result supports using question generation and answering as an automatic bridge from a broad language instruction to more frequent learning signals.
neurips-2022-eager-asking-and-answering-.tldr: EAGER turns language goals into automatically generated questions and rewards trajectories that answer them, improving sample efficiency in BabyAI.

paragraphs: Solving numerical problems expressed in text requires understanding the passage and constructing the right calculations. Many approaches represent those calculations as programs. This paper identifies a design issue in earlier methods: generating operators and operands together can restrict their ability to construct programs for complicated reasoning tasks.

ELASTIC separates these responsibilities within an adaptive symbolic compiler. A RoBERTa encoder processes the input, while the compiler contains a Reasoning Manager, Operator Generator, Operands Generator, and Memory Register. Distinguishing the operation from the values it uses gives the program generator a more structured organization. The framework also supports expanding the available operators without tying that expansion to a fixed number of operands, which underlies its claimed domain flexibility.

The reported FinQA results are 68.96 execution accuracy and 65.21 program accuracy, while MathQA program accuracy reaches 83.00. The authors report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art models. These findings support the compiler design as an effective approach to the numerical reasoning tasks evaluated.
neurips-2022-elastic-numerical-reasoning.tldr: ELASTIC separates operator and operand generation in a symbolic compiler, improving numerical reasoning results on FinQA and MathQA.

paragraphs: Long-term forecasting requires a model to preserve useful information from the past without fitting the noise mixed into that history. This paper argues that historical representation still leaves considerable room for improvement, even with strong recurrent and Transformer models. FiLM addresses that issue by combining a structured memory of past observations with frequency-based processing.

The model uses projections onto Legendre polynomials to approximate historical information. It then applies Fourier projection to remove noise and incorporates a low-rank approximation to accelerate computation. These components address related requirements: representing the history, reducing distracting variation, and keeping the resulting computation manageable. The method therefore focuses on how the past is stored and processed for future prediction.

The empirical study reports accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art models of 19.2% for multivariate forecasting and 22.6% for univariate forecasting. The authors also demonstrate that the representation module can improve other deep learning modules when used as a plugin. This extends the contribution beyond the complete FiLM model.
neurips-2022-film-frequency-improved-leg.tldr: FiLM combines Legendre memory, Fourier-based noise removal, and low-rank computation to improve long-term time-series forecasting.

paragraphs: Language descriptions can help an agent learn what to do, but connecting complex descriptions to observations is difficult when rewards arrive rarely or late. Language Dynamics Distillation addresses this grounding problem by learning from demonstrations before reinforcement learning begins. Its pretraining task predicts environment dynamics from demonstrations accompanied by language.

The resulting language-aware representations are then fine-tuned through reinforcement learning. Training aims both to increase expected reward and to retain knowledge of how language relates to changes in the environment. This makes the connection between descriptions and dynamics part of the representation the policy learns to use, rather than leaving that connection entirely dependent on delayed task rewards.

On SILG's five tasks, which assess different generalization challenges in unseen environments, LDD outperforms learning from scratch, VAE pretraining, and the compared methods using unlabeled demonstrations. Additional analyses find that language in demonstrations improves sample efficiency and generalization across environments. They also find expert demonstrations more effective than non-expert demonstrations for dynamics modeling.
neurips-2022-improving-policy-learning-v.tldr: LDD pretrains language-aware dynamics representations from demonstrations and improves policy learning and generalization on the SILG benchmark.

paragraphs: Interaction-Grounded Learning studies how an agent can improve its behavior without receiving an explicit reward. The learner observes a context, chooses an action, and receives a feedback vector. Its objective is to use these interactions to optimize a policy with respect to a reward function that remains latent, rather than directly supplied.

A problem with previously analyzed approaches is that they fail when the feedback itself contains the action. This is a meaningful obstacle for potential brain-computer and human-computer interface applications, where feedback may include information about what the system did. The paper introduces an algorithm and analysis that accommodate action information in the feedback, regardless of how that action is encoded.

The authors support the approach with theoretical guarantees and large-scale experiments constructed from supervised datasets. These results demonstrate effectiveness in the studied setting while expanding the feedback structures that IGL can handle. The contribution concerns learning from action-inclusive feedback; the cited interface applications provide motivation rather than reported deployment evidence.
neurips-2022-interaction-grounded-learni.tldr: The paper extends Interaction-Grounded Learning to feedback that contains the chosen action, with theoretical guarantees and dataset-based experiments.

paragraphs: Data augmentation relies on knowing which changes to an input should leave its output unchanged. Choosing the corresponding augmentation parameters often takes human effort and repeated validation. This paper develops a gradient-based method that learns those choices during neural-network training without needing a separate validation dataset.

The approach treats augmentation as an invariance encoded in a prior over the functions a neural network can represent. That formulation makes Bayesian model selection a way to learn which invariances fit the data. To make the objective usable for deep networks, the authors construct a differentiable, Kronecker-factored Laplace approximation to marginal likelihood. Differentiability allows the augmentation parameters to be adjusted through gradient optimization.

The authors show that their method can recover invariances present in the data and improve generalization and data efficiency on image datasets. The contribution extends an idea previously demonstrated for Gaussian processes to deep neural networks. Its practical significance is learning augmentation settings from the training process itself, reducing reliance on manual selection and validation-based tuning.
neurips-2022-invariance-learning-in-deep.tldr: A differentiable Bayesian model-selection objective learns neural-network augmentation invariances without validation data, improving image-learning results.

paragraphs: Recognizing a new object category from only a few examples requires representations that transfer beyond their training categories. This paper proposes Deep Object Patch Encodings, or DOPE, to learn detailed object representations without category labels or semantic labels for object parts. The training signal comes from observing the same object instance from multiple viewpoints.

DOPE assumes access to sparse depth information, foreground masks, and known cameras. Together, these allow the method to establish pixel-level correspondences between views. Those correspondences define a self-supervised task for learning discriminative object patches. The method therefore replaces category annotation with geometric information that connects observations of an object across images.

The learned descriptors can be used directly for low-shot classification of novel categories by matching local parts. The authors report results competitive with, and outperforming, supervised and self-supervised baselines. The findings support learning transferable category information through local visual correspondence, with the stated geometric inputs providing the supervision needed to train the representation.
neurips-2022-learning-dense-object-descr.tldr: DOPE learns object-patch descriptors from multiview geometric correspondences and uses local matching for low-shot recognition of new categories.

paragraphs: An energy network makes a prediction by optimizing an energy function that describes relationships between inputs and outputs. Training then evaluates that prediction with a loss. This creates a difficult gradient calculation: changing the network parameters changes the solution of the prediction-time optimization problem, and conventional training often needs to differentiate through that solution.

The paper introduces generalized Fenchel-Young losses to address this difficulty. Its mathematical starting point is a generalized conjugate function that replaces the usual bilinear pairing with a general energy function. The resulting losses are designed for learning energy networks, and their gradients can be computed efficiently without differentiating the argmin or argmax operation used to obtain a prediction.

The authors also prove an excess-risk calibration result for linear-concave energies, connecting the loss construction to predictive performance under that condition. They demonstrate the losses on multilabel classification and imitation learning. The contribution combines a more tractable training calculation with a conditional theoretical guarantee and examples in two application settings.
neurips-2022-learning-energy-networks-wi.tldr: Generalized Fenchel-Young losses enable efficient energy-network gradients without argmin or argmax differentiation, with calibration proved for linear-concave energies.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should be labeled next. Look-ahead strategies assess candidates by considering how the model would change if it were retrained with each possible labeled example. This can provide a more informative selection criterion, but repeatedly retraining a deep network makes the procedure computationally demanding.

The paper uses the neural tangent kernel to approximate the results of that hypothetical retraining. It proves that the approximation works asymptotically even within an active learning setup, enabling look-ahead criteria with much less computation. The same approach also supports sequential updates in a streaming setting without running stochastic gradient descent after every newly added example.

The proposed querying strategy considers how additional data would alter predictions. In the reported pool-based experiments, it outperforms other look-ahead strategies by large margins and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks. These findings support the practical value of approximating future model changes, while the theoretical approximation guarantee specifically has an asymptotic scope.
neurips-2022-making-look-ahead-active-le.tldr: Neural tangent kernels approximate hypothetical retraining, making look-ahead active learning cheaper and competitive on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Learning from large, varied collections of trajectories could give decision-making agents reusable knowledge before task-specific training. Masked decision prediction, or MaskDP, pursues this idea through self-supervised pretraining for reinforcement learning and behavioral cloning. It applies masked autoencoding to sequences containing states and actions.

During pretraining, the method randomly hides state and action tokens and asks the model to reconstruct them. Filling those gaps requires extracting information about dynamics from the surrounding trajectory. The authors find that using different masking proportions substantially helps the model learn representations that generalize across multiple downstream tasks.

In the empirical study, MaskDP transfers without task-specific training to new behavioral-cloning tasks involving single and multiple goals, and infers skills from a few example transitions. It also transfers well to offline reinforcement learning and shows promising behavior as model size increases. With data-efficient fine-tuning, it achieves results competitive with autoregressive pretraining methods. Together, these findings support masked trajectory reconstruction as a reusable pretraining objective for decision making.
neurips-2022-masked-autoencoding-for-sca.tldr: MaskDP reconstructs masked states and actions to learn transferable representations for behavioral cloning and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Flow models generate molecules by reversing an encoding process. Existing approaches can introduce artificial dequantization, depend on particular node or edge orderings, lack permutation invariance, or create discrepancies between encoding and decoding that require later validity corrections. This paper develops a flow-based molecular generator intended to avoid these issues.

Inspired by partial differential equations on graphs, the method uses continuous normalizing flows built from coupled differential equations for graph nodes. These flows are E(3)-equivariant, meaning their behavior respects the corresponding spatial transformations. Local updates repeatedly reconcile densities toward global alignment. The authors also express the models as message-passing temporal networks, connecting their continuous dynamics to communication between graph nodes.

The paper reports strong density estimation and molecular generation, with generated samples reaching state-of-the-art results on QM9 and ZINC250K. Those findings support the proposed coupled-flow construction on two standard molecular benchmarks. The contribution combines the generative role of invertible flows with structural design choices aimed at avoiding the representational and decoding problems identified in earlier models.
neurips-2022-modular-flows-differential-.tldr: Modular Flows uses coupled, equivariant continuous dynamics for molecular generation, reporting state-of-the-art samples on QM9 and ZINC250K.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization must find promising inputs through evaluations, even when different regions of the search space behave very differently. Tree-based approaches can organize that space and balance exploring uncertain regions against exploiting promising ones. This paper extends that approach by integrating sample-based descent more deeply into Monte Carlo tree search.

The authors develop new tree-expansion mechanisms and descent methods at tree vertices, combining stochastic search with Gaussian processes. They also design rules for branch selection, uncertainty versus progress, and propagating information back through the tree. Localized Gaussian processes provide auxiliary guidance for exploration and exploitation, while the search puts greater emphasis on sampling that can produce faster descent.

Experiments show that the proposed algorithms can outperform state-of-the-art methods on many challenging benchmark problems. This is an empirical finding rather than a universal claim about every black-box objective. The main contribution is a coordinated search procedure in which regional organization and local improvement work together to accelerate progress toward good solutions.
neurips-2022-monte-carlo-tree-descent-fo.tldr: Monte Carlo Tree Descent combines tree search, stochastic descent, and localized Gaussian processes to improve black-box optimization on many benchmarks.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search is often evaluated on familiar image-classification tasks, leaving its usefulness in other domains unclear. NAS-Bench-360 addresses this evaluation gap with ten tasks covering different applications, dataset sizes, dimensionalities, and learning objectives. Each task is selected to work with modern convolutional-network search methods, including outside the domains where those methods were developed.

For two tasks, the authors release precomputed performance results for 15,625 architectures from a standard convolutional search space. These results reduce the computation needed to study architecture-search methods. The suite also provides a setting for testing whether hypotheses developed in the NAS literature continue to hold across a broader range of problems.

The experiments find inconsistent performance among several modern NAS procedures across the ten tasks, including many extremely poor results. This makes success on familiar benchmarks insufficient evidence of reliable performance across these diverse tasks. The contribution is both an evaluation resource and evidence that architecture-search research benefits from testing across a wider range of learning problems.
neurips-2022-nas-bench-360-benchmarking-.tldr: NAS-Bench-360 evaluates architecture search across ten diverse tasks and reveals substantial inconsistency in several modern methods.

paragraphs: Social-media face filters are widely used, but studying their effects quantitatively is difficult without accessible collections of filtered images. The paper identifies proprietary platforms and limited access to filter implementations as obstacles. It also rejects scraping faces from those platforms as an ethically acceptable way to assemble research data.

OpenFilter provides a framework for applying filters available on social-media platforms to existing large collections of face images. This gives researchers a way to create filtered datasets from existing image resources. The approach directly addresses the shortage of research material that has constrained psychological, artistic, and sociological analysis of these widely used visual transformations.

The authors also release FairBeauty and B-LFW, beautified versions of the public FairFace and LFW datasets, and outline insights from analyzing them. These resources make the framework's contribution concrete: researchers gain both a method for applying filters and datasets containing the resulting transformations. The stated contribution supports quantitative study of filter effects without establishing any particular psychological or social outcome in the abstract.
neurips-2022-openfilter-a-framework-to-d.tldr: OpenFilter applies social-media face filters to existing image collections and releases two beautified datasets to support research.

paragraphs: Estimating the poses of several people requires locating keypoints while preserving each person's spatial structure. Existing end-to-end methods use dense representations for this detail, but can introduce redundant and complex inference post-processing. QueryPose proposes a sparse framework that predicts multiple people's keypoint sequences directly from an image.

Each person is represented by an instance-level query associated with several learnable queries for body parts. A Spatial Part Embedding Generation Module uses local spatial attention to produce embeddings containing spatial and structural information. A Selective Iteration Module then updates the part queries adaptively, stage by stage. Together, these modules give the sparse queries information needed for precise keypoint prediction.

QueryPose uses bipartite matching to avoid hand-designed post-processing. The reported results reach 73.6 AP on MS COCO mini-val and 72.7 AP on the CrowdPose test set, surpassing the compared dense end-to-end methods. These findings support part-level queries as a way to retain useful spatial detail within a sparse pose-regression framework.
neurips-2022-querypose-sparse-multi-pers.tldr: QueryPose uses spatially informed part queries to predict multiple human poses directly, outperforming compared dense methods on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Some differentially private optimization problems require sampling distributions that closely match a target at every point. This paper studies that requirement for log-concave distributions constrained to a convex body. Its infinity-distance criterion bounds the largest absolute log density ratio, imposing pointwise control beyond what a total-variation guarantee alone provides.

Previous infinity-distance sampling bounds depended polynomially on inverse error, whereas total-variation sampling could achieve polylogarithmic dependence. When the target's negative log density is Lipschitz, the proposed algorithm obtains infinity-distance error at most epsilon using a number of membership and function-evaluation oracle calls polynomial in dimension and log inverse error. This substantially improves the stated dependence on requested accuracy.

The method converts continuous samples with total-variation guarantees into samples with infinity-distance guarantees, departing from approaches based on fine discretizations of the domain. For convex bodies that are polytopes, combining this conversion with Dikin Walk bounds also improves dimension dependence. The contribution links a more accessible sampling guarantee to the stronger guarantee needed by the motivating applications.
neurips-2022-sampling-from-log-concave-d.tldr: A continuous-sample conversion achieves infinity-distance guarantees with polylogarithmic inverse-error oracle complexity under the stated Lipschitz assumption.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy reconstructs protein structures from noisy two-dimensional projections taken at unknown poses. Data containing multiple structural states make reconstruction particularly challenging. Variational autoencoders can help represent this variation, but coordinate-based reconstructions in Fourier space do not inherit all the advantages that similar representations offer in ordinary spatial reconstruction.

This paper instead expresses the VAE reconstruction on a volumetric grid. It makes that representation efficient to train through a backpropagation method that exploits the sparsity of the Fourier-space projection operation. The change connects the reconstruction representation and its training procedure: a grid becomes practical because gradient computation takes advantage of the structure of the projection.

Compared with the coordinate-based approach, the method improves results on a simulated dataset and achieves at least equivalent results on an experimental dataset, while substantially reducing computational cost. The efficiency gain is especially strong during inference. That enables users to interactively analyze the latent space, making exploration of the learned structural variation more practical.
neurips-2022-sparse-fourier-backpropagat.tldr: Grid-based VAE reconstruction with sparse Fourier backpropagation reduces cryo-EM computation while matching or improving the reported reconstruction results.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can support text generation by addressing exposure bias or making use of non-parallel datasets. Its effectiveness depends heavily on the reward function, yet existing rewards are often specific to a task and provide sparse feedback. This paper proposes deriving a more broadly applicable reward from a model already trained with teacher forcing.

The resulting reward is step-wise, providing feedback throughout generation rather than relying only on a sparse task signal. The approach is task-agnostic in its construction, so the reward comes from the trained model instead of a separately designed task-specific function. The authors also introduce a simple modification intended to stabilize reinforcement learning on non-parallel datasets when using this induced reward.

Experiments across several text-generation tasks show improvements over self-training and reward-regression methods. These findings support the usefulness of the recovered reward for the evaluated tasks. The contribution connects an existing supervised training procedure to reinforcement learning by turning the teacher-forced model into a source of ongoing generation feedback.
neurips-2022-teacher-forcing-recovers-re.tldr: A teacher-forced model supplies task-agnostic, step-wise rewards that improve reinforcement learning for several text-generation tasks.

paragraphs: A predictive distribution describes uncertainty that a single best guess cannot express. Evaluating such predictions one input at a time, however, does not establish how well a model represents uncertainty across several inputs together. The Neural Testbed is an open-source benchmark designed to examine both individual, marginal predictions and joint predictions.

The authors evaluate a range of prediction-generating agents using a simple neural-network data-generating process. This provides a controlled setting for assessing their uncertainty estimates. Some popular Bayesian deep learning agents produce accurate marginal predictions but perform poorly on joint predictions, showing that success on the first evaluation does not ensure success on the second.

The study also finds that joint-prediction quality drives performance in downstream decision tasks. The reported findings remain robust across a wide range of generative models. This gives joint evaluation a practical motivation: uncertainty relationships across inputs can affect decisions even when predictions for each input look good in isolation. The benchmark makes those relationships an explicit part of assessment.
neurips-2022-the-neural-testbed-evaluati.tldr: The Neural Testbed shows that accurate per-input uncertainty can coexist with poor joint predictions that matter for downstream decisions.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer opportunities for energy-efficient computing, but training deep versions efficiently remains challenging, particularly for analog hardware. This paper introduces Local Tandem Learning, a teacher-student approach that uses a pretrained artificial neural network to guide the training of a spiking network.

The student learns to mimic intermediate feature representations from its teacher. By separating the learning of different layers and supplying informative supervisory signals, the method reduces training complexity. On CIFAR-10, the authors demonstrate rapid convergence within five training epochs. They also report that the trained spiking networks achieve accuracies comparable to their teacher networks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet.

The proposed rule is designed to suit hardware implementation as well as model training. The authors describe its use for on-chip parameter calibration and robustness to non-ideal device behavior. These properties make the method relevant to mixed-signal neuromorphic chips, where a practical learning rule must cope with the behavior of physical computing components as well as deliver useful predictions.
neurips-2022-training-spiking-neural-net.tldr: Local Tandem Learning trains spiking networks from intermediate teacher features, achieving rapid convergence and teacher-comparable accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Unsupervised detector pretraining needs signals that teach a model where objects are and how to distinguish them. Earlier approaches often produce these object priors with separate heuristics, leaving prior generation disconnected from detector learning. This paper proposes generating the priors from the detector itself and improving both together.

The framework combines two sources of information. Encoder attention maps supply region priors that emphasize foreground areas, while selected high-quality decoder bounding boxes supply instance priors. Under the assumption that objects are instances within the foreground, these signals jointly define the object priors. As detector optimization proceeds, the priors are refined too, creating a feedback process in which better supervision can improve detection and better detection can improve supervision.

In COCO low-data detection settings, the method improves over competitive approaches by 1.3 AP with 1% of the data and 1.7 AP with 10%. These results support jointly learning object priors and detection capabilities as a useful pretraining strategy when labeled data are limited.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-object-detecti.tldr: Jointly refining model-generated object priors and detector learning improves detection in the reported COCO low-data settings.
